title: Cut and Join Copper Pipe
summary: Cut copper water pipe cleanly and join it with solder, push-to-connect or press fittings: to fix a pinhole leak, replace a section, or connect to PEX. You'll end with tight, leak-tested joints.
safety: Shut off and drain the water first. When soldering: shield wood and insulation, keep a fire extinguisher and spray bottle in reach, wear glasses and gloves, ventilate, and stay 30 minutes after the last joint to watch for hidden fire. Use only lead-free solder and flux on drinking water pipe.
pro: the main shutoff won't close, the pipe is badly corroded or has several pinholes, you'd be soldering in a tight spot near wood or wiring you can't shield, the work is a gas line (never use this guide for gas), or your area requires a permit or licensed plumber for work inside walls.

calcNote: Joints assume two pipe ends per fitting (a tee has three). Solder is about one pipe-diameter of wire per joint plus extra for practice. Pipe includes 20% for mistakes.

For pipe close to a wall or joist where a full-size cutter can't spin.

Cleans the outside of the pipe to bright copper.
Cleans the inside of fitting sockets.
Keeps the joint clean while heating so solder can flow.
A small 1/2 lb spool is plenty. Never use 50/50 lead solder on water pipe.

tools.w: MAPP heats faster (best for 3/4"); propane is fine for 1/2".
Protects wood, wiring and insulation behind the joint.
Within arm's reach whenever the torch is lit.
Wets wood around the joint and knocks down sparks.
The pipe stays hot well away from the joint.
Solder and flux can spit when hot.
Catch draining water and wipe joints.

tools.w: Mark cuts and insert depths.
Only if you're replacing a section. Type L is thicker than M and a good default.

steps.t: Identify your pipe and plan the job
steps.idea: You can't buy the right fittings until you know the pipe's size and type.
steps.b:
1. Find the part you'll work on. Look for printing along the pipe: it says the type (K, L or M) and size.
  2. No printing? Wrap a strip of paper around the pipe, mark the overlap, and measure the length. About 2" around (5/8" across) = 1/2" pipe. About 2-3/4" around (7/8" across) = 3/4" pipe.
  3. Check the stripe color if any: red = type M (thin), blue = type L (thicker), green = type K (thickest). You join all three the same way.
  4. Count the fittings you need (couplings, elbows, tees) and buy a spare or two.
  5. Is the pipe green-crusted, flattened or full of pinholes? Expect more leaks nearby. Replace a longer section.
faq: Is it copper or something else?
Copper is reddish-brown, bends a little, and a magnet won't stick. Gray pipe that a magnet sticks to is galvanized steel, which needs different fittings and often a pro.
Can I mix 1/2" and 3/4"?
Yes, with a reducing fitting (for example a 3/4" x 1/2" coupling). Don't shrink a main line just to make the job easier: it lowers flow to everything after it.

steps.idea: Solder is cheapest and permanent, push-fit needs no flame, press is the pro's choice.
steps.b:
1. Solder (sweat): a torch melts solder into the joint. Cheapest fittings, permanent, but needs a dry pipe and fire precautions. Practice on scrap first.
  2. Push-to-connect: deburr, mark, push. No heat, works on wet pipe, removable. Each fitting costs several times more.
  3. Press: a powered tool squeezes a fitting with an O-ring. Fast and flame-free, but the tool costs hundreds; most homeowners hire a plumber who has one or rent it.
  4. Your current choice: {{a.method==='sweat'?'solder':a.method==='push'?'push-to-connect':'press'}}. Change it in the questions above if you like.
faq: Are push-fit fittings allowed inside walls?
Many brands are listed for concealed use, but some local codes or inspectors want an access panel at any push-fit fitting. Check the package and your local code; when in doubt, keep them accessible.
Do I need to practice soldering?
Yes. Buy a 2 ft scrap and three couplings and do six joints before you touch the house. It costs a few dollars and saves a flood.

steps.t: Shut off the water and drain the lines
steps.idea: The pipe must be empty: you can't cut, solder or push-fit against house pressure.
steps.b:
1. Find the main shutoff valve, usually where the water line enters the house (basement, crawlspace, garage, or by the water heater). Turn it clockwise until it stops, or turn a lever handle so it sits across the pipe.
  2. If there's a closer shutoff that isolates only your section, use it instead.
  3. Open the highest faucet in the house (top floor) to let air in.
  4. Open the lowest tap (basement sink, laundry, or outdoor spigot) to let water out. Wait until it stops running.
  5. Working on a hot-water pipe? Set the water heater to VACATION or PILOT (gas) or turn off its breaker (electric), and close its cold inlet valve.
  6. Put a bucket and towels under the spot where you'll cut.
steps.stop: If the main valve won't turn, is crusty or drips at the stem, don't force it: old valves break. Call the water utility to shut it at the curb, or a plumber.
faq: The water won't stop completely.
The main valve may not seal fully (common with old gate valves). A slow drip is OK for push-fit, not for solder. See the drip step, or replace the main valve with a pro's help.
Why turn off the water heater?
An electric heater's elements can burn out if the tank isn't full, and you don't want to scald yourself on a hot pipe.

steps.idea: Prepare for fire before you light the torch, not after.
steps.b:
1. Clear anything that burns away from the joint: boxes, rags, paper insulation, plastic.
  2. Hang a flame-protector cloth or metal shield between the joint and any wood, wiring or insulation within about 12".
  3. Mist the wood around the joint with the spray bottle.
  4. Set the fire extinguisher on the floor within reach, pin in place, label facing you.
  5. Open a window or run a fan: flux fumes are irritating.
  6. Keep the flame well away from plastic pipe (PEX, CPVC), plastic valves and wire insulation. Shield them or wrap them in a wet rag.
steps.stop: Never point a flame at insulation, paper-faced drywall or a joist without a shield. Fiberglass facing and dust in joist bays ignite and can smolder unseen.
faq: Do I need a permit?
Repairs are usually allowed without a permit, but rules vary. Some areas require permits for any work inside walls or new piping. Check your local code.

steps.idea: Cut out only as much as needed, but get past any damaged copper.
steps.b:
1. Dry the pipe with a rag. With water still on (before draining), find where the drip starts. Water runs along pipe, so the spot you see wet may be lower than the hole.
  2. Mark the hole with a marker.
  3. Mark cut lines about 1/2" on each side of the hole. For a long split, mark past both ends of it.
  4. Check that each side has at least 2" of straight, round pipe for the coupling to slide over (no fitting in the way).
  5. Now shut off and drain (previous step).
faq: Can I just wrap it with tape or a clamp?
A rubber-lined pipe repair clamp is a fine emergency fix until you can do this properly. Epoxy putty and tape are not permanent.
The pipe has several pinholes.
Pinholes often mean the pipe wall is thinning from the inside. Fix this one, then have a plumber look at the water chemistry and the rest of the pipe.

steps.idea: A tubing cutter makes a square cut without crushing the pipe.
steps.b:
1. Measure and mark the cut all the way around if you can.
  2. Open the cutter and set the wheel exactly on the mark. Tighten the knob until the wheel just touches.
  3. Spin the cutter one full turn around the pipe. It should leave a thin line that meets itself.
  4. Tighten the knob about a quarter turn. Spin again. Repeat until the pipe snaps apart.
  5. Hold the bucket under it: there's always a little water left.
  6. No room to spin? Use a mini cutter, which needs about 1" of clearance around the pipe.
faq: The cut spirals instead of meeting.
The wheel isn't square to the pipe. Back off, realign on the mark, start with lighter pressure.
Can I use a hacksaw?
In a pinch, but it leaves a ragged, crooked end that's hard to seal. File it square and deburr well.

steps.t: Stop a pipe that won't stop dripping
steps.idea: Solder won't flow while water trickles in. Stop the water or switch to a fitting that doesn't care.
steps.b:
1. Open a faucet that's lower than your joint. Often that alone empties the line.
  2. Still trickling? Tear a soft slice of white bread (no crust), roll it into a loose ball and push it into the pipe end, a few inches back from the joint.
  3. Do your joint quickly. When the water returns, the bread dissolves and washes out through a faucet; remove faucet aerators first so it can't clog them.
  4. Still won't stop? Use a push-fit fitting for this one joint.
faq: Is the bread trick really OK?
It's an old plumber's trick and works for a slow trickle. Clean aerators afterward. Never use anything that won't dissolve, like a rag.

steps.idea: Removing the cut's sharp lip lets water flow freely and keeps O-rings from tearing.
steps.b:
1. Push the cone of the reamer (often a fold-out blade on the cutter) into the pipe end.
  2. Twist it a few times until the inside edge is smooth and the opening looks full size.
  3. Run emery cloth or a file around the outside edge to knock off any sharp ridge.
  4. Wipe out any copper shavings.
faq: Is this really needed?
Yes. A burr makes turbulence that wears through copper over years, and on push-fit it can slice the O-ring and cause a leak.

steps.t: Clean pipe and fitting to bright copper
steps.idea: Solder only sticks to clean, bare metal.
steps.b:
1. Wrap emery cloth around the pipe end and twist back and forth over the last 1" until it's evenly bright.
  2. Push the fitting brush into each socket of the fitting and twist until the inside shines.
  3. Blow or tap off grit.
  4. Don't touch the cleaned areas with your fingers.
faq: How clean is clean?
Bright pink-orange all around, like a new penny. Dull or dark spots will leave a gap in the solder.

steps.idea: Flux keeps the copper clean while it heats; a dry fit proves everything lines up before heat.
steps.b:
1. Stir the flux. Brush a thin, even coat on the cleaned pipe end.
  2. Brush a thin coat inside the fitting socket.
  3. Push the pipe into the fitting and twist a quarter turn to spread the flux. It should bottom out against the stop inside.
  4. Fit every piece of the section together and check angles and lengths. Wipe off any flux that squeezed out.
  5. Solder within the same session: flux left for days can corrode the pipe.
faq: Can I use more flux to be safe?
No. Excess flux runs inside the pipe and can cause pinhole corrosion later. A thin film is enough.

steps.idea: Heat the fitting so it pulls solder into the joint.
steps.stop: Check the shield and extinguisher are in place. Keep the flame away from plastic pipe, wires, and your other hand.
steps.b:
1. Unroll about 6" of solder and bend the last 1" into an L.
  2. Light the torch and point the tip of the small inner blue cone at the middle of the fitting.
  3. Move the flame slowly back and forth over the fitting, not the pipe.
  4. After 10–30 seconds the flux will sizzle and then go clear or start to smoke lightly.
  5. Touch the solder to the joint on the side opposite the flame. If it melts on contact, go to the next step. If not, heat a few seconds more.
faq: MAPP or propane?
Propane works fine on 1/2". MAPP-type gas burns hotter and is quicker on 3/4" and on joints near valves or other fittings. Either works with a self-igniting head.
The flux turned black.
You overheated it. Let it cool, take it apart, clean and flux again. Solder won't stick to burned flux.

steps.idea: Capillary action pulls melted solder into the thin gap, toward the heat.
steps.b:
1. Pull the flame back slightly or move it to the far side of the fitting.
  2. Touch the solder to the seam where pipe enters fitting. It should melt and get sucked in.
  3. Feed solder around the seam. You need only about as much solder as the pipe's size: about 1/2" of wire for 1/2" pipe, 3/4" for 3/4" pipe.
  4. Stop when a thin silver ring shows all the way around and a drip starts to form.
  5. Solder both ends of a coupling, heating the middle once.
faq: Solder drips out the bottom.
Too much solder or too much heat. A small drip is harmless; brush it off while soft.
Solder won't go in on one side.
That spot wasn't clean or hot enough. Heat that side and try again. If it still won't take, take the joint apart hot (with pliers), clean, flux, and redo.

steps.idea: Don't move the joint until the solder has hardened.
steps.b:
1. Turn off the torch and set it down on a flat, fireproof surface, flame side away from anything.
  2. While still warm (not hot), wipe the joint with a damp rag to remove flux. Careful: it's hot enough to burn.
  3. Don't bump, bend or cool the joint with water. Let it cool on its own for about 5 minutes.
  4. Mist any wood that got warm.
faq: How do I know it's good?
A smooth, shiny, continuous ring of solder all the way round. Gaps, lumps or a dull, grainy look are suspect. The real test is turning the water back on.

steps.idea: The mark proves the pipe went all the way through the O-ring and grab ring.
steps.b:
1. Make sure the end is cut square and deburred, with no scratches in the last inch.
  2. Clean off paint, corrosion or solder with emery cloth so the O-ring seals on smooth copper.
  3. Slide the depth gauge over the pipe end (or measure the depth from the fitting's chart).
  4. Draw a line all the way around at the gauge's edge.
faq: The old pipe has solder on it.
Cut back to clean pipe or sand the solder off completely. Push-fit only seals on smooth, round pipe.

steps.idea: Push straight in until the mark meets the fitting. That's the whole joint.
steps.b:
1. Hold the fitting square to the pipe.
  2. Push firmly with a slight twist until the pipe hits the stop. You'll feel it seat.
  3. Check that your depth mark is right at the edge of the fitting.
  4. Tug back on the fitting. It shouldn't come off.
  5. To remove: push the disconnect clip against the release collar, hold it in, and pull the fitting off.
steps.stop: If the mark is more than about 1/16" away from the fitting, it's not seated and will leak or blow off. Push it on further.
faq: Can I reuse a push-fit fitting?
Most makers allow it a few times if the O-ring and teeth are undamaged, but a new one is cheap insurance.
It spins on the pipe. Is that wrong?
No. Most push-fit fittings can rotate after they're on. That's normal.

steps.idea: A press tool crimps the fitting around an O-ring in seconds, with no flame.
steps.b:
1. Cut square and deburr. Clean the pipe end so it's smooth.
  2. Mark the insert depth (from the fitting maker's chart) on the pipe.
  3. Check the O-ring is seated in the fitting and not twisted.
  4. Push the pipe in until the mark is at the fitting edge.
  5. Put the correct size jaw square over the fitting's bead and pull the trigger. The tool runs a full cycle.
  6. Many fittings have a "leak before press" feature or a tag that falls off: remove tags so you can see which joints are done.
[[info|Call a pro|Press tools are expensive and need jaws matched to the fitting brand. If you don't want to rent one, hire a plumber; a few joints take them minutes.]]
faq: Can I use a regular crimper?
No. Copper press fittings need a powered press tool with the matching jaw profile.

steps.idea: A slip coupling has no inner stop, so it can slide over the gap where you cut out the leak.
steps.b:
1. Cut out the damaged piece at your marks (no more than the coupling can cover; most leave room for a 1" gap). Deburr and clean both ends.
  2. Measure half the coupling length and mark that distance back from each pipe end.
  3. {{a.method==='push'?'Push the slip coupling fully onto one pipe end until the far end of the coupling reaches the mark the maker shows for sliding.':'Flux both ends and inside the coupling, then slide it all the way onto one pipe.'}}
  4. Line the pipes up, then slide the coupling back across the gap until each end sits at your mark: centered over the gap.
  5. {{a.method==='push'?'Check both depth marks are at the coupling ends.':'Solder both ends as in the solder steps.'}}
faq: The pipes won't line up.
Loosen nearby pipe straps a little so the pipe can move, then retighten after.
Can I use a regular coupling?
Only if one pipe can be pulled sideways enough to slip it in, which is rare in a wall. That's what the slip coupling is for.

steps.idea: An adapter lets you continue the run in flexible PEX tubing.
steps.b:
1. {{a.method==='sweat'?'Solder the copper-by-PEX adapter onto the copper first, with no PEX attached.':'Push a push-fit coupling onto the copper (it accepts both pipe types).'}}
  2. {{a.method==='sweat'?'Let it cool completely, until you can hold it bare-handed.':'Push a PEX stiffener insert into the PEX end if the fitting needs one (many come with it in place).'}}
  3. Connect the PEX with the method that matches the adapter: crimp ring, cinch clamp, or push-fit.
  4. Keep PEX at least 18" away from where you'll use the torch, and from any water heater flue (check the PEX maker's rules).
faq: Can I solder with PEX attached?
No. Heat will melt or weaken PEX. Always solder first and let it cool.

steps.t: Turn the water on and check for leaks
steps.idea: Fill the pipes slowly to avoid hammer, then inspect every joint.
steps.b:
1. Remove the aerators (screw-off tips) of the faucets you opened, so debris can flush out.
  2. Close the lowest tap. Leave the top faucet open.
  3. Open the main valve a quarter of the way. Listen to the pipes fill.
  4. When water runs steady from the top faucet with no spitting air, close it and open the main fully.
  5. Wipe each new joint dry, then hold dry tissue underneath for a minute. It must stay dry.
  6. Check again after 30 minutes and again the next day before closing any wall.
  7. Run each faucet briefly, then clean and replace the aerators. Turn the water heater back on last, once its tank is full.
steps.stop: A leaking solder joint can't be fixed by adding solder with water in the pipe. Shut off, drain, take it apart, clean and redo it.
faq: A push-fit joint leaks.
It's almost always not fully seated, has a scratched pipe, or a burr. Shut off, remove it, check the end and depth mark, and push it on again.
The pipes bang when I turn the water on.
Trapped air or water hammer. Open faucets to bleed air. Re-secure loose pipe straps.

steps.idea: Hidden fires from torch work show up after you've stopped. Stay and check.
steps.b:
1. Stay in the area for at least 30 minutes after your last joint.
  2. Feel the wood and shield near each joint with your hand and sniff for smoke a few times.
  3. Once the joints are cool, wipe off any remaining flux residue with a damp rag.
  4. Let the torch head cool before storing. Close the cylinder valve if it has one.
faq: Why 30 minutes?
Wood or dust that got scorched can smolder slowly and burst into flame later. Most torch fires happen after the plumber has packed up.

cutHelp.b:
1. Open the cutter and set the wheel on your mark.
  2. Tighten until the wheel just touches the pipe.
  3. Spin it one full turn around the pipe.
  4. Tighten about a quarter turn, spin again. Repeat until it cuts through.
  5. Too much pressure dents the pipe so fittings won't slide on.

deburrHelp.b:
1. Insert the reamer cone into the pipe.
  2. Twist until the inside lip is gone.
  3. Smooth the outside edge with emery cloth.
  4. Shake out any shavings.

cleanHelp.b:
1. Emery cloth around the pipe end, 1" back, until bright.
  2. Fitting brush inside each socket until bright.
  3. No fingers on cleaned copper.

torchHelp.b:
1. Screw the torch head onto the cylinder hand-tight. Sniff for gas; no smell, no hiss.
  2. Shield, spray bottle and extinguisher in place.
  3. Point it away from you, open the valve, pull the trigger to light.
  4. Aim the tip of the inner blue cone at the fitting.
  5. Shut the valve fully when you set it down.

pushHelp.b:
1. Square cut, deburred, smooth pipe end.
  2. Mark the insert depth with the gauge.
  3. Push straight in to the mark.
  4. Tug to check. Use the clip to remove.

deburr.cap: Every cut leaves a small curled lip inside the pipe. Ream it away until the inside edge is smooth and full size.

clean.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Clean to bright copper</text><rect x="10" y="56" width="150" height="28" class="w"/><rect x="104" y="56" width="56" height="28" class="y"/><text x="132" y="100" class="k" text-anchor="middle">1" shiny</text><text x="12" y="100">dull / oxidized</text><rect x="110" y="44" width="44" height="10" rx="2" class="th"/><text x="132" y="38" text-anchor="middle">emery cloth</text><rect x="190" y="50" width="70" height="40" rx="4" class="tb"/><rect x="232" y="58" width="28" height="24" class="y"/><rect x="268" y="66" width="44" height="8" rx="2" class="bk"/><line x1="240" y1="62" x2="240" y2="78" class="o"/><line x1="245" y1="62" x2="245" y2="78" class="o"/><line x1="250" y1="62" x2="250" y2="78" class="o"/><line x1="255" y1="62" x2="255" y2="78" class="o"/><line x1="260" y1="62" x2="260" y2="78" class="o"/><text x="225" y="108" text-anchor="middle">fitting brush</text><text x="225" y="120" text-anchor="middle">inside the socket</text><text x="10" y="140">Shine where solder or the seal will sit.</text><text x="10" y="152" class="wa">Then hands off: skin oil stops solder.</text>
clean.cap: Rub until the copper is evenly bright like a new penny, on the pipe end and inside the fitting socket.

flux.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Flux: a thin, even coat</text><rect x="10" y="62" width="160" height="30" class="w"/><rect x="120" y="60" width="50" height="34" rx="3" class="th"/><g transform="rotate(-30 190 60)"><rect x="176" y="36" width="70" height="8" rx="2" class="y"/><rect x="166" y="34" width="12" height="12" rx="2" class="th"/></g><text x="145" y="112" class="k" text-anchor="middle">thin coat, 1" long</text><rect x="210" y="62" width="100" height="30" rx="2" class="w"/><rect x="250" y="56" width="60" height="42" rx="3" class="badf" opacity=".35"/><text x="260" y="112" class="wa" text-anchor="middle">too thick: drips,</text><text x="260" y="124" text-anchor="middle">pits the pipe later</text><text x="10" y="148">Coat the pipe end AND inside the fitting.</text>
flux.cap: Flux keeps the cleaned copper from re-oxidizing while you heat it. Use a lead-free, water-soluble paste and a small brush, never your finger.

heat.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Heat the fitting, not the solder</text><rect x="10" y="80" width="300" height="24" class="w"/><rect x="120" y="72" width="80" height="40" rx="4" class="tb"/><line x1="160" y1="72" x2="160" y2="112" class="o d"/><rect x="146" y="166" width="28" height="30" rx="4" class="bk"/><path d="M160 166 C140 150 146 128 160 116 C174 128 180 150 160 166z" class="y"/><path d="M160 166 C152 156 154 146 160 138 C166 146 168 156 160 166z" class="af"/><text x="200" y="148" class="ac">tip of the inner blue</text><text x="200" y="160">cone touches the</text><text x="200" y="172">fitting, middle-ish</text><text x="10" y="140">Sweep the flame</text><text x="10" y="152">over the fitting</text><text x="160" y="62" class="k" text-anchor="middle">solder goes on the far side</text>
heat.cap: The hottest spot of a torch flame is just past the tip of the small blue inner cone. Put that on the fitting body, not on the solder.

solder.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Capillary action pulls solder in</text><rect x="10" y="74" width="300" height="10" class="w"/><rect x="10" y="116" width="300" height="10" class="w"/><rect x="100" y="60" width="120" height="14" class="tb"/><rect x="100" y="126" width="120" height="14" class="tb"/><line x1="160" y1="60" x2="160" y2="140" class="o d"/><rect x="100" y="72" width="0" height="4" class="th"><animate attributeName="width" values="0;58;58" keyTimes="0;0.7;1" dur="3s" repeatCount="indefinite"/></rect><rect x="100" y="124" width="0" height="4" class="th"><animate attributeName="width" values="0;58;58" keyTimes="0;0.7;1" dur="3s" repeatCount="indefinite"/></rect><line x1="88" y1="40" x2="100" y2="58" class="o" style="stroke-width:3"/><text x="10" y="36">solder wire touches the joint</text><line x1="110" y1="98" x2="150" y2="98" class="a"/><polygon points="150.0,98.0 143.7,101.0 143.7,95.0" class="af"/><text x="168" y="102" class="ac">solder flows in toward</text><text x="168" y="114" class="ac">the heat, filling the gap</text><text x="10" y="166">Done when a silver ring shows all the way around.</text>
solder.title: Watch solder wick in
solder.cap: If the joint is hot enough, solder melts on contact and disappears into the gap. If it balls up and rolls off, the fitting is not hot yet.

shield.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Protect the wall before you light up</text><rect x="10" y="30" width="18" height="150" class="w"/><rect x="140" y="30" width="18" height="150" class="w"/><rect x="28" y="30" width="112" height="150" class="b" opacity=".35"/><text x="84" y="46" text-anchor="middle">wood + insulation</text><rect x="44" y="60" width="80" height="80" rx="3" class="y"/><text x="84" y="96" class="k" text-anchor="middle">heat</text><text x="84" y="108" class="k" text-anchor="middle">shield</text><rect x="10" y="140" width="160" height="12" class="w"/><circle cx="96" cy="146" r="9" class="tb"/><text x="190" y="60" class="k">Fire cloth or metal</text><text x="190" y="72">shield behind joint</text><text x="190" y="96" class="k">Spray bottle of</text><text x="190" y="108">water in reach</text><text x="190" y="132" class="k">ABC extinguisher</text><text x="190" y="144">within arm's reach</text><text x="10" y="198" class="wa">Stay and check for 30 min after the last joint.</text>
shield.cap: Most torch fires start smoldering inside a wall or joist bay and show up after you leave. Shield it, wet it, and watch it.

bread.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">A trickle of water ruins a solder joint</text><rect x="10" y="60" width="140" height="22" class="w"/><rect x="20" y="64" width="110" height="14" class="wt"/><path d="M150 70 q8 0 8 14 q0 6 -4 6 q-4 0 -4 -6z" class="wt"/><text x="10" y="104" class="wa">water turns to steam and</text><text x="10" y="116" class="wa">blows the solder out</text><rect x="180" y="60" width="130" height="22" class="w"/><rect x="250" y="64" width="40" height="14" class="th"/><rect x="190" y="64" width="50" height="14" class="wt"/><text x="270" y="56" class="k" text-anchor="middle">bread</text><text x="180" y="104" class="gd">soft bread, no crust,</text><text x="180" y="116">holds water back, then</text><text x="180" y="128">dissolves later</text><text x="10" y="156">Better fixes: open a lower faucet, or use</text><text x="10" y="168">a push-fit fitting, which works on wet pipe.</text>
bread.cap: You cannot solder a pipe with water in it. Stop the trickle first or switch that joint to push-fit.

depth.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Push-fit: mark the depth, push to it</text><rect x="150" y="50" width="120" height="70" rx="6" class="tb"/><rect x="160" y="62" width="10" height="46" class="y"/><rect x="180" y="60" width="8" height="50" rx="2" class="badf" opacity=".6"/><line x1="210" y1="50" x2="210" y2="120" class="o" style="stroke-width:3"/><rect x="30" y="70" width="180" height="30" class="w"/><line x1="150" y1="66" x2="150" y2="104" class="o" style="stroke-width:3"/><line x1="30" y1="66" x2="30" y2="104" class="o d"/><text x="124" y="140" class="gd" text-anchor="middle">mark: shows at the edge</text><line x1="150" y1="130" x2="150" y2="106" class="good"/><polygon points="150.0,106.0 153.0,112.3 147.0,112.3" class="goodf"/><text x="165" y="42" text-anchor="middle">grab ring</text><text x="214" y="138">stop</text><text x="10" y="160">1/2" pipe goes in about 7/8"; 3/4" about 1".</text><text x="10" y="172">Use the gauge or chart from the maker.</text><text x="196" y="42">O-ring</text>
depth.cap: Mark the insert depth on the pipe before you push. When the fitting is fully on, the mark sits right at the fitting edge.

slip.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Fix a pinhole with a repair coupling</text><text x="10" y="36" class="wa">BEFORE</text><rect x="10" y="44" width="300" height="20" class="w"/><circle cx="160" cy="54" r="3" class="badf"/><path d="M160 64 q-4 8 0 12 q4 -4 0 -12" class="wt"/><line x1="140" y1="40" x2="140" y2="68" class="bad d"/><line x1="180" y1="40" x2="180" y2="68" class="bad d"/><text x="190" y="36" class="wa">cut out about 1"</text><text x="10" y="100" class="gd">AFTER</text><rect x="10" y="108" width="128" height="20" class="w"/><rect x="182" y="108" width="128" height="20" class="w"/><rect x="110" y="102" width="100" height="32" rx="4" class="tb"/><line x1="110" y1="140" x2="110" y2="146" class="o"/><line x1="210" y1="140" x2="210" y2="146" class="o"/><line x1="110" y1="146" x2="210" y2="146" class="o"/><text x="160" y="160" text-anchor="middle">centered over the gap</text><text x="10" y="182">Slip coupling: no stop inside, so it slides</text><text x="10" y="194">all the way on, then back to center.</text>
slip.cap: Mark half the coupling length on each pipe end so you can see it is centered. Each end must cover at least the full socket depth.

pex.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Changing from copper to PEX</text><rect x="10" y="60" width="110" height="20" class="w"/><text x="10" y="52">copper</text><rect x="118" y="54" width="54" height="32" rx="4" class="tb"/><text x="145" y="104" class="k" text-anchor="middle">adapter</text><rect x="170" y="62" width="140" height="16" rx="3" class="m"/><text x="310" y="52" text-anchor="end">PEX</text><text x="10" y="128">Push-fit: copper in one side, PEX (with its</text><text x="10" y="140">stiffener insert) in the other.</text><text x="10" y="160">Solder: sweat a copper-by-PEX adapter, let it</text><text x="10" y="172">cool fully, THEN crimp or clamp the PEX.</text>
pex.cap: Never heat near PEX. Solder the adapter first and let it cool, or use a push-fit transition with no heat at all.

test.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Turn water on slowly, then look</text><circle cx="60" cy="80" r="34" class="bk"/><line x1="60" y1="80" x2="60" y2="52" class="o" style="stroke-width:4"/><path d="M60 40 a40 40 0 0 1 36 22" class="a"/><polygon points="96,62 88,58 98,54" class="af"/><text x="60" y="136" class="k" text-anchor="middle">main: open a little</text><text x="60" y="148" text-anchor="middle">at a time</text><rect x="150" y="70" width="160" height="20" class="w"/><rect x="200" y="64" width="50" height="32" rx="4" class="tb"/><rect x="212" y="102" width="26" height="14" rx="2" class="bk"/><text x="225" y="128" text-anchor="middle">dry tissue</text><text x="150" y="52" class="k">wipe dry, then check each joint</text><text x="150" y="146" class="wa">Any drop? Water off,</text><text x="150" y="158" class="wa">drain, redo the joint.</text>
test.cap: Bleed air at a faucet as the pipes fill. Then hold dry tissue under each joint. A wet spot shows a leak too small to see.

glossary: Sweat / solder
Joining copper by heating a fitting and melting solder into the joint.
Flux
A paste that cleans and protects copper while it's heated so solder can flow.
Capillary action
The way liquid is pulled into a very narrow gap. It draws melted solder into the joint.
Burr
The sharp lip left inside a pipe after cutting.
Type M / L / K
Copper wall thickness: M is thinnest (red print), L medium (blue), K thickest (green).
Nominal size
The trade name of the pipe size (1/2", 3/4"). The outside is 1/8" bigger.
Push-to-connect
A fitting with an O-ring and grab ring that seals when you push the pipe in.
Press fitting
A fitting with an O-ring that is crimped onto the pipe with a powered press tool.
Slip (repair) coupling
A coupling with no stop inside, so it can slide along the pipe to bridge a gap.
MAPP
A hotter-burning torch gas than propane, sold in yellow cylinders.
PEX
Flexible plastic water tubing, often red, blue or white.
